{{Short description|Dimension of a subset of a metric space}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''packing dimension''' is one of a number of concepts that can be used to define the [[dimension]] of a [[subset]] of a [[metric space]].  Packing dimension is in some sense [[duality (mathematics)|dual]] to [[Hausdorff dimension]], since packing dimension is constructed by "packing" small [[open ball]]s inside the given subset, whereas Hausdorff dimension is constructed by covering the given subset by such small open balls. The '''packing dimension''' was introduced by C. Tricot Jr. in 1982.

==Definitions==

Let (''X'',&nbsp;''d'') be a metric space with a subset ''S''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''X'' and let ''s''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0 be a real number.  The ''s'''''-dimensional packing pre-measure''' of ''S'' is defined to be

:<math>P_0^s (S) = \limsup_{\delta \downarrow 0}\left\{ \left. \sum_{i \in I} \mathrm{diam} (B_i)^s \right| \begin{matrix} \{ B_i \}_{i \in I} \text{ is a countable collection} \\ \text{of pairwise disjoint closed balls with} \\ \text{diameters } \leq \delta \text{ and centres in } S \end{matrix} \right\}.</math>

Unfortunately, this is just a [[pre-measure]] and not a true [[measure (mathematics)|measure]] on subsets of ''X'', as can be seen by considering [[dense set|dense]], [[countable set|countable]] subsets.  However, the pre-measure leads to a ''bona fide'' measure: the ''s'''''-dimensional packing measure''' of ''S'' is defined to be

:<math>P^s (S) = \inf \left\{ \left. \sum_{j \in J} P_0^s (S_j) \right| S \subseteq \bigcup_{j \in J} S_j, J \text{ countable} \right\},</math>

i.e., the packing measure of ''S'' is the [[infimum]] of the packing pre-measures of countable covers of ''S''.

Having done this, the '''packing dimension''' dim<sub>P</sub>(''S'') of ''S'' is defined analogously to the Hausdorff dimension:

:<math>\begin{align}
\dim_{\mathrm{P}} (S) &{}  = \sup \{ s \geq 0 | P^s (S) = + \infty \} \\
&{} = \inf \{ s \geq 0 | P^s (S) = 0 \}.
\end{align}</math>

===An example===
The following example is the simplest situation where Hausdorff and packing dimensions may differ.

Fix a sequence <math>(a_n)</math> such that <math>a_0=1</math> and <math>0<a_{n+1}<a_n/2</math>. Define inductively a nested sequence <math>E_0 \supset E_1 \supset E_2 \supset \cdots</math> of compact subsets of the real line as follows: Let <math>E_0=[0,1]</math>. For each connected component of <math>E_n</math> (which will necessarily be an interval of length <math>a_n</math>), delete the middle interval of length <math>a_n - 2a_{n+1}</math>, obtaining two intervals of length <math>a_{n+1}</math>, which will be taken as connected components of <math>E_{n+1}</math>. Next, define <math>K = \bigcap_n E_n</math>. Then <math>K</math> is topologically a Cantor set (i.e., a compact totally disconnected perfect space). For example, <math>K</math> will be the usual middle-thirds Cantor set if <math>a_n=3^{-n}</math>.

It is possible to show that the Hausdorff and the packing dimensions of the set <math>K</math> are given respectively by:

:<math>\begin{align}
\dim_{\mathrm{H}} (K) &{}  = \liminf_{n\to\infty} \frac{n \log 2}{- \log a_n} \, , \\
\dim_{\mathrm{P}} (K) &{}  = \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{n \log 2}{- \log a_n} \, .
\end{align}</math>

It follows easily that given numbers <math>0 \leq d_1 \leq d_2 \leq 1</math>, one can choose a sequence <math>(a_n)</math> as above such that the associated (topological) Cantor set <math>K</math> has Hausdorff dimension <math>d_1</math> and packing dimension <math>d_2</math>.

===Generalizations===

One can consider [[dimension function]]s more general than "diameter to the ''s''": for any function ''h''&nbsp;:&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;+∞)&nbsp;→&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;+∞], let the '''packing pre-measure of''' ''S'' '''with dimension function''' ''h'' be given by

:<math>P_0^h (S) = \lim_{\delta \downarrow 0} \sup \left\{ \left. \sum_{i \in I} h \big( \mathrm{diam} (B_i) \big) \right| \begin{matrix} \{ B_{i} \}_{i \in I} \text{ is a countable collection} \\ \text{of pairwise disjoint balls with} \\ \text{diameters } \leq \delta \text{ and centres in } S \end{matrix} \right\}</math>

and define the '''packing measure of''' ''S'' '''with dimension function''' ''h'' by

:<math>P^h (S) = \inf \left\{ \left. \sum_{j \in J} P_0^h (S_j) \right| S \subseteq \bigcup_{j \in J} S_j, J \text{ countable} \right\}.</math>

The function ''h'' is said to be an '''exact''' ('''packing''') '''dimension function''' for ''S'' if ''P''<sup>''h''</sup>(''S'') is both finite and strictly positive.

==Properties==
* If ''S'' is a subset of ''n''-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> with its usual metric, then the packing dimension of ''S'' is equal to the upper modified box dimension of ''S'': <math display="block">\dim_{\mathrm{P}} (S) = \overline{\dim}_\mathrm{MB} (S).</math> This result is interesting because it shows how a dimension derived from a measure (packing dimension) agrees with one derived without using a measure (the modified box dimension).

Note, however, that the packing dimension is ''not'' equal to the box dimension.  For example, the set of [[rational number|rationals]] '''Q''' has box dimension one and packing dimension zero.
